extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / general early-18th-century literate public interested in moral and satirical essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and embedded evaluative principles for composing short moral/satirical periodical essays (Spectator-style), including what subjects and rhetorical methods are effective and what personal behaviours are to be commended or censured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content is equivalent to Wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Content is equivalent to Wealth; Luxury to Poverty; 'Content is natural Wealth', 'Luxury is artificial Poverty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract your desires and consider yourself rich when you have more than you want. Avoid always looking to those richer than yourself; keep wishes within your fortunes. Examples: Pittacus thanking the King of Lydia because he already had more by half than he knew what to do with; middle sorts who live within their means are the truly wealthy. Scoring note: measures of 'wealth' are psychological (satisfaction) as much as material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire content by counting surplus
rubrics_metrics.description: First of all, A Man should always consider how much he has more than he wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparison with your own possessions (focus on what you still have) to generate contentment. Anti-pattern: foolish men focus on what they have lost or on those richer than themselves. Example/illustration: Aristippus's reply when condoled about losing a farm — he still had three farms vs the other's one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire content by imagining worse states
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondly, How much more unhappy he might be than he really is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alleviate current misfortune by comparing it to greater possible calamities. Use small anecdotes or aphorisms (e.g., the Dutchman: 'It was a great Mercy that 'twas not his Neck') to reframe pain. Examples: Dr. Hammond's practice of thanking God that when he had the gout it was not the stone, and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as effective means to contentment
rubrics_metrics.description: There was never any System besides that of Christianity, which could effectually produce... the Virtue I have been hitherto speaking of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that religion uniquely prescribes means to better one’s condition and gives consolatory promise of future reward, thus making contentment more attainable than philosophical rationalizations that merely 'silence' but do not satisfy. Anti-pattern: relying solely on abstract philosophical arguments that may produce despair rather than consolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singularity is laudable when grounded in conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Singularity is laudable, when, in Contradiction to a Multitude, it adheres to the Dictates of Conscience, Morality, and Honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a writer or person opposes the majority on grounds of duty, morality, or truth, that singularity is 'heroick Bravery' and praiseworthy. Rule of action: follow duty, not custom. Use such moral courage as a positive trait in characterization or argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singularity is vicious when contrary to reason or trivial
rubrics_metrics.description: Singularity therefore is only vicious when it makes Men act contrary to Reason, or when it puts them upon distinguishing themselves by Trifles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between principled dissent and mere affectation: eccentricity in dress, behaviour, or petty matters (e.g., insisting on strictly true formalities, wearing a turban to be 'wholsome') is ridiculous and should be censured or satirized. Practical test: is the deviation from custom serving conscience/honour or merely aiming to be different?

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to custom in indifferent matters
rubrics_metrics.description: In these Cases there is a certain Deference due to Custom; and ... a Man ought to sacrifice his private Inclinations and Opinions to the Practice of the Publick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In indifferent, non-moral particulars (dress, hours, small civilities) authors should recommend conforming to social practice to avoid useless singularity; emphasize social prudence and the pragmatic benefits of conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the desire not to appear singular (fashionability danger)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is indeed nothing which betrays a Man into so many Errors and Inconveniences, as the Desire of not appearing singular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn against excessive desire to seem fashionable (or to fit in) because it leads to affectations, overindulgence, and vice. Use cautionary anecdote: the 'lively' young man who tried to be fashionable and 'died of old Age at Five and twenty' as satirical hyperbole showing the costs of that pursuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anecdotes, classical quotations and examples to teach or satirize
rubrics_metrics.description: The essays rely on short stories, classical sayings, and vivid examples (Aristippus, Pittacus, Bion, Dutchman, Doctor Hammond) to illustrate moral points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical guideline for essayists: support abstract maxims with memorable anecdotes and classical authorities; employ irony and concise stories to both entertain and instruct. Anti-pattern: dry abstraction without concrete exempla—this may 'silence' rather than satisfy the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish levels of importance when judging behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Singularity in things of no Importance, as in Dress, Behaviour, Conversation, and all the little Intercourses of Life... should be assessed differently than singularity in matters of conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing moral critique or satire, weigh the significance of the subject: reserve strong censure for moral failings, allow indulgence or recommend conformity in trivial social matters. Example: the North English gentleman's philosophical oddities warranted guardianship though he 'did no Harm'—but ridicule is the suitable tone.
